if you hope and long for the experience of God's goodness
then you yourselves must be ready to exercise goodness. In
your lament over your own distresses there must not be
mingled any note of complaining that others are better
treated than you; there must not be intermixed with your
sorrows any suggestion of mean envy. Rather, if we wish to
experience joy ourselves, we must be ready to rejoice with
others. And it is remarkable how, in our joy over the good
fortune of others, our own troubles find some alleviation.
If we are able to rejoice with others in their happiness, we
inwardly participate in the good which has been bestowed on
them. Then we are permitted to see the manifestation of
God's goodness, and to become aware of God's goodness in its
manifestations is always an enheartening and strengthening
experience. And it is just the man who can see God's good-
ness reflected in the lives of others, who has also eyes to see
it when it comes to himself. But if we cannot rejoice in the
blessings which enrich other lives, then we make ourselves
blind to those which come to ourselves.
Was this not in fact the case with those men who were first
hired? Had they not essentially a great advantage over those
who were not hired until eventide? Certainly they had borne
the burden of work the whole day through. But could this
fact be viewed from one side only, namely, work as a torment
and burden? Was it not possible to look at the situation in
another light also? Those who were hired later were not
idlers and loafers, but simply workless men. Is it the case
that the unemployed have so much better a lot than those
who are at work? Should not rather those who are in work
feel obliged to give thanks and rejoice because they are able
to work?

own experience. My father was for many years the parson of
a village in the district where I was brought up. When I
returned to this village some years later, I fell into conversa-
